subject: Whether extracting billing from the Rails monolith into a separate service is the right and feasible way to meet audit finding AF-2026-09's 'logical segregation' requirement by 30 April 2027, including effort and schedule risk
decisionObjective: The exec meeting needs to decide how to close audit finding AF-2026-09 by 30 April 2027. That means choosing between full service extraction and cheaper controls the auditor also accepts (database-level access controls, separate schemas with restricted roles, segregation of duties, audit logging), and judging how likely each option is to finish in time. The request asks for an exact engineer-month figure and a firm yes/no. The plan has no phase estimates and the coupling analysis is incomplete, so the evaluation should produce a defensible range with explicit uncertainty and the conditions that would turn it into a yes or a no. It should not invent false precision.

criteria.name: Fit to the audit requirement
criteria.rationale: AF-2026-09 asks for restricted access to billing data and code paths, segregation of duties and change audit logging, and it explicitly does not prescribe an architecture. The option chosen has to produce controls the auditors can see working. A finished extraction that lacks access controls and audit logging would still fail, and lighter options may be enough.

criteria.name: Schedule feasibility against 30 April 2027
criteria.rationale: The exec wants a yes/no on meeting the deadline. Planned staffing is 4 engineers at 50% from January, which is about 2 FTE over roughly 4 months, or about 8 engineer-months of capacity before the deadline. That capacity has to be compared with realistic effort, including dual-write and cutover phases that cannot be compressed.

criteria.name: Effort estimate credibility, calibrated to history
criteria.rationale: The three past extractions overran their estimates by about 1.8x, 2.6x and 2.4x. Any engineer-month figure has to be adjusted for this record and stated as a range, not one exact number.

criteria.name: Scope and coupling uncertainty
criteria.rationale: 214 files reference Billing::, shared tables have not been analysed, and the background-job scan is incomplete (at least 17 jobs). These unknowns drive both the effort and the risk of a failed cutover, and they are what currently make an exact estimate impossible.

criteria.name: Delivery readiness and execution risk
criteria.rationale: The plan has no owner, every phase is marked TBD, and staffing is part-time. Weak governance makes slippage more likely and affects whether a firm commitment is credible at all.

criteria.name: Fallback and interim compliance path
criteria.rationale: If extraction overruns, the company needs interim controls such as DB roles, schema separation or audit logging that can satisfy the auditors by the deadline while extraction continues, so that missing the deadline does not mean failing the audit.

assumptionsToVerify.assumption: Extracting billing into its own service is needed, or is the right way, to satisfy the auditors' 'logical segregation' requirement.
assumptionsToVerify.howToCheck: Compare against the text of AF-2026-09, which says no architecture is prescribed and DB-level controls or separate schemas are acceptable. Confirm with the auditors what evidence they expect.

assumptionsToVerify.assumption: An exact engineer-month figure can be produced for the extraction.
assumptionsToVerify.howToCheck: Check whether bottom-up phase estimates and a complete coupling analysis exist. Currently all phases are TBD and the dependency analysis is partial, so only a range calibrated to history can be justified.

assumptionsToVerify.assumption: A firm yes/no on completion before 30 April 2027 can be given.
assumptionsToVerify.howToCheck: Compare calibrated effort ranges with confirmed capacity. Report a probability or conditional answer unless the range sits entirely above or below the available capacity.

assumptionsToVerify.assumption: The audit deadline is 30 April 2027 and the requirement is 'logical segregation'.
assumptionsToVerify.howToCheck: Confirm the deadline date and wording against the formal audit finding or the auditor correspondence. The attached finding does not state a date.

assumptionsToVerify.assumption: Staffing of 4 engineers at 50% from January gives about 8 engineer-months before the deadline.
assumptionsToVerify.howToCheck: Recompute from confirmed start date, allocation, holidays and on-call load. Confirm with engineering leadership that these engineers are committed.

assumptionsToVerify.assumption: The historical overrun ratios (18/10=1.8, 13/5=2.6, 16.8/7=2.4) apply to the billing extraction.
assumptionsToVerify.howToCheck: Recompute the ratios from estimate-history.csv and check that the past projects are comparable in scope, team and coupling.

evidenceByGap.question: What exactly will the auditors accept as evidence of 'logical segregation' by 30 April 2027? Would database-level access controls or separate schemas with restricted roles, plus segregation of duties and change audit logging, fully close AF-2026-09 without extracting a service?

evidence.claim: Audit finding AF-2026-09 requires that access to billing data and billing code paths be restricted to authorised roles, with segregation of duties and audit logging of changes. It states that the auditors do not prescribe an architecture, and that database-level access controls, separate schemas with restricted roles, or service extraction are all acceptable if the controls are demonstrable.
evidence.applicability: G1 and the assumption that extraction is required. The finding's own text says extraction is not necessary, so lighter controls can close the finding if they are demonstrable.
evidence.limitations: This is a two-sentence summary, not the full finding. It does not define what 'demonstrable' evidence is, it names no testing period, and it does not say whether the auditor wants the controls operating effectively over a period or only designed and implemented.

evidence.claim: The user states that the auditors require billing to be 'logically segregated' from the Rails monolith by 30 April 2027, and that engineering leadership wants to extract billing into its own service to satisfy this.
evidence.applicability: The deadline and the framing of the requirement. Neither the phrase 'logically segregated' nor the date 30 April 2027 appears in the supplied audit-finding.md, which also says extraction is not required.
evidence.limitations: The deadline and wording could not be checked against the formal finding or auditor correspondence. The supplied finding contains no date.

evidence.claim: pgAudit is a PostgreSQL extension that provides session audit logging (statements by class, e.g. READ, WRITE, DDL) and object audit logging (statements affecting particular relations, controlled through pgaudit.role, limited to SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE). Its stated goal is 'to produce audit logs often required to comply with government, financial, or ISO certifications.' The README states 'pgAudit supports PostgreSQL 14 or greater' and 'Audit logging is best-effort and not transactional.'
evidence.applicability: G1 and C6. Database-level change audit logging on billing tables is available off the shelf and does not require extracting a service, which supports a lighter or interim compliance path.
evidence.limitations: This only applies if the monolith uses PostgreSQL, and the supplied documents do not name the database engine. 'Best-effort and not transactional' could matter for audit evidence. A search snippet said PostgreSQL 13+, while the fetched README says 14+, so the version floor depends on the README version. Database audit logs do not cover code-path access or segregation of duties in deployment on their own.

evidence.claim: PostgreSQL GRANT gives no public access by default for tables, columns and schemas. The schema USAGE privilege lets a role look up objects in a schema, and each object's own privileges still apply. Roles can be granted to other roles. Superusers bypass object privileges.
evidence.applicability: G1 and C6. Separate schemas with restricted roles are a standard database mechanism and match the option the finding explicitly accepts.
evidence.limitations: Search snippet only. The WebFetch of www.postgresql.org failed (host not allowed in this session's network settings). The two refs are an official page and a vendor mirror of the same documentation, so they are not truly independent, and this is kept at INFERRED. The superuser bypass means segregation of duties also has to cover who holds superuser or DBA access. Applicable only if the database is PostgreSQL.

evidence.claim: Practitioner and exam-prep sources describe ITGC audit evidence for logical access (access listings, tickets, approvals, review sign-offs), segregation of duties (role matrices showing requester, approver and administrator are different people; developers without production deploy rights) and change management (sampled change tickets with authorisation, testing and deployment segregation). They note that SoD gaps and missing change approvals are frequent causes of findings.
evidence.applicability: G1 and G6. Auditors typically test whether controls are operating, through access reviews, approvals and logs, rather than the system's architecture. A 'finished' extraction without these controls would not by itself produce the evidence auditors sample.
evidence.limitations: Based only on search-result summaries; no page was fetched. Most sources are not primary standards (PCAOB AS 2201, COBIT and NIST 800-53 were not inspected). This is general practice and cannot stand in for confirmation from this company's auditor.

evidence.claim: The Rails 'Multiple Databases with Active Record' guide (main-branch source) says each abstract class owns the connection for one database (or one writer/replica pair). connects_to should be defined on a single abstract class per database, and models stored in that database inherit from it. connects_to can only be called on ActiveRecord::Base or abstract classes; calling it on a concrete model raises NotImplementedError. connected_to switches role for a block, and the role must match one defined by connects_to. The guide says 'Rails does not create database users; create writer and read-only replica users in your database system', and that Rails' read-only check 'is not a substitute for database permissions.' Listed limits: no SQL joins across separate database clusters (disable_joins: true loads associations with separate queries instead), 'Rails does not provide distributed transactions across database clusters', and database-level foreign keys generally cannot span separate clusters.
evidence.applicability: D1, G1 and C6. Rails supports giving billing models their own connection with a separate database credential (an abstract BillingRecord with connects_to pointing at a database.yml entry with a restricted user). This is the standard mechanism for role separation inside a single Rails app. The access restriction itself comes from database grants, not from Rails. The DB users and grants have to be set up outside Rails.
evidence.limitations: Fetched via WebFetch, which returns a summary from a small model, so the quoted phrases may be lightly paraphrased. This is the main-branch guide, which may differ from the Rails version the monolith runs; the Rails version is not in the supplied documents. The guide's join, transaction and FK caveats are written for separate database clusters. Whether they apply in the same way to two connections with different users on one database is not stated; see E14.

evidence.claim: Several Rails sources describe one app using several database entries with different usernames: the Rails 6.0 guide configures primary and replica entries with different users, where the replica user has read-only permissions, and a GoCardless engineering write-up uses an abstract base class with connects_to that concrete models inherit from. A Rails forum thread notes that establish_connection in a model gives a per-model connection, not per-query user switching.
evidence.applicability: D1. Separate credentials are bound per model class hierarchy, not per code path or per caller. Any non-billing code that touches a billing model (controllers, the 17+ invoice jobs, the 214 referencing files) still goes through the billing connection and credential. So a separate billing DB role restricts which tables non-billing models can reach. It does not on its own restrict which code paths can call billing models. Code-path restriction still needs code ownership, review and deploy controls, or an API or module boundary.
evidence.limitations: Search snippets except the GitHub guide (E12). The forum threads are old (around 2008). The point that a per-class credential does not restrict callers is a reasoned implication of the documented per-class model, not a statement in the sources.

evidence.claim: Inference: introducing a restricted billing DB role inside the monolith carries its own refactoring and migration risk, driven by the same unknowns as extraction. If billing tables are granted only to a billing role, any non-billing model, query, join, report or background job that reads or writes those tables through the main connection will fail at runtime, so each such path has to be found and either moved onto the billing connection or explicitly granted. Shared tables (not yet analysed) need an ownership decision. Work that today runs in one transaction across billing and non-billing tables would span two connections and lose atomicity unless restructured. Moving tables into a separate schema also means migrations and search_path or table-name changes.
evidence.applicability: D1 and D4, G2 and C6. This undercuts any claim that the lighter path has 'no data-migration or cutover risk'. The lighter path still needs a billing write-path and shared-table inventory (E4) before its effort can be estimated. It does avoid dual-write ledger synchronisation and a service cutover. A staged rollout is possible: first add a billing role with grants plus audit logging while the app still connects with broad rights, then tighten grants once access paths are known. That is design reasoning, not a sourced practice.
evidence.limitations: Reasoned from E4, E12 and E13; no source measures this effort. The size of the problem depends entirely on the shared-table and write-path inventory, which does not exist. The database engine and the current credential setup of the monolith are not stated (E22).

evidence.claim: GitLab's split of CI tables into a separate database within its Rails monolith needed systematic remediation. SQL joins across the CI and non-CI databases do not work. Cross-joins were handled by allowlisting failing specs and fixing each case before removing allow_cross_joins_across_databases. Foreign keys spanning the databases were removed and replaced with 'loose foreign keys', an eventually consistent async cleanup, which GitLab warns can cause user-visible latency problems. GitLab's handbook describes the CI data as relatively loosely coupled, which kept changes minimal.
evidence.applicability: D1. This is a real-world precedent: separating a domain's data access inside a large Rails monolith means finding and fixing every cross-domain join, transaction and foreign key. That is the same coupling work billing would need under either option. It applies most directly to a full separate-database split. A same-database restricted-role approach keeps joins possible for roles that hold both grants, but not for a role without billing grants.
evidence.limitations: Search snippets only; no page fetched, and no effort figure (person-months or sprints) was found. All refs are GitLab-owned domains, so they are not independent and this stays INFERRED. The GitLab split was a separate physical database, a stronger separation than schema or role restriction.

evidence.claim: PostgreSQL row security: superusers and roles with the BYPASSRLS attribute always bypass row security. Table owners normally bypass it too unless ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set. Practitioner guides recommend that the application connection role should not be a superuser, should not have BYPASSRLS and should not own the protected tables (or FORCE must be set). They also recommend policies with both USING and WITH CHECK, so that writes are restricted as well as reads.
evidence.applicability: D1. Row-level security restricts rows, mainly for tenant isolation. It is not needed to separate a whole domain's tables, where schema and table GRANTs (E7) are enough. The key practical point carries over to GRANT-based separation as well: if the Rails app connects as a superuser or as the table owner (common when the same credential runs migrations), DB-level restrictions are bypassed. A separate migration or owner role, distinct from the runtime roles, would be needed, and segregation of duties has to cover who holds it.
evidence.limitations: Search snippets only; the postgresql.org fetch failed earlier in this run (host not allowed) and the bytebase.com fetch also failed. The claim that Rails apps often connect as table owner is reasoned, not sourced. This applies only if the database is PostgreSQL.

evidence.claim: For SOC 2 Type II, several sources state that the AICPA sets no explicit minimum observation period. In practice 3 months is described as the industry-standard minimum accepted by most auditors (Bastion), often used for a first report. About 6 months is commonly recommended for a first Type II, and shorter periods get more scrutiny from buyers.
evidence.applicability: D4, G1 and C6. If AF-2026-09's auditor expects Type II-style operating evidence, controls have to run for a period before the deadline, and 3 months is the shortest commonly accepted window. Counting back 3 months from 30 April 2027 would put go-live at about 31 January 2027. A 6-month window would have needed go-live by about 31 October 2026, which is already past on 11 Nov 2026. This date arithmetic is the researcher's and should be rechecked downstream.
evidence.limitations: Vendor and consultancy blogs, not the AICPA itself; snippets only (the bastion.tech fetch failed: host not allowed). AF-2026-09 does not say whether the audit is SOC 2, SOX/ICFR, internal audit or something else, and it names no testing period (E1). The window is set by agreement with the auditor.

evidence.claim: Expel states that 'according to AICPA, Type 2 requires a minimum 6-month observation window.'
evidence.applicability: D4. If an auditor held to a 6-month window, controls would have needed to be live by about end of October 2026, so a fully operating-effective period before 30 April 2027 would already be out of reach. The likely fallback would be design-and-implementation evidence plus a partial period, or a negotiated date.
evidence.limitations: Single search snippet. It conflicts with the other sources (E17), which say the AICPA sets no minimum, so the attribution to the AICPA is doubtful.

evidence.claim: For SOX/ICFR remediation, sources say a remediated or newly designed control must operate for a 'sufficient period of time' before management or auditors can conclude it is effective, and a newly designed control that has not operated long enough cannot support a conclusion that a weakness is remediated. The length is a judgement call. Practitioner blogs say that in practice most auditors expect at least one full quarter of operation, or 'typically a minimum of 3 months'. Sources also note that late go-lives leave no operating period for testing before year end.
evidence.applicability: D4. This supports a go-live target of roughly end of January 2027 for the lighter controls (one quarter before 30 April 2027) if the auditor wants operating evidence. Earlier is better if quarterly controls such as access reviews have to show more than one occurrence.
evidence.limitations: Search snippets from practitioner and consultancy sources. The SEC 2007 interpretive guidance and PCAOB AS 2201 were not inspected. The search summary did not reliably say which source gave the 'one quarter' versus the '3 months' figure, so I kept this at INFERRED even though several domains appear. It applies only if the audit is ICFR-type.

evidence.claim: Practitioner sample-size guidance for testing control operating effectiveness varies by frequency, and sources disagree somewhat. One gives annual 1, quarterly 2 to 3, monthly 2 to 4, weekly 5 to 15. Another gives quarterly 2-4, monthly 2-5, weekly 5-15, daily 20-25. A third gives one for annual, two for quarterly, two to five for monthly. New controls not tested in prior periods are listed as a factor calling for larger samples.
evidence.applicability: D4. Planner inference: a quarterly user-access review needs at least 2 occurrences to be sampled, which takes about two quarters. A control that first runs in late January 2027 could show only one quarterly occurrence by 30 April 2027. Change-management and deploy controls that run often (per change) can produce enough samples within weeks. This favours running the first access review early and choosing per-change or monthly cadences.
evidence.limitations: Search snippets only; the ranges conflict across sources and are not standards. Which source gave which range was not confirmed. The 'two quarters' implication is reasoning, not a sourced statement.

evidence.claim: Planner inference: under a roughly 3-month operating window, the lighter-controls path has about 11.5 weeks from 11 Nov 2026 to an end-of-January 2027 go-live. Planned staffing starts only in January (E3), so redirecting it to the lighter path would leave about one month of 2-FTE capacity before that target unless work starts earlier. Components to land by then include a billing DB role and grants (with a separate migration/owner role), audit logging (e.g. pgAudit), an SoD matrix, code-ownership and deploy restrictions on billing paths, and a first access review. All are subject to the write-path and shared-table inventory in E14.
evidence.applicability: D4, G5 and C2/C6. This is the feasibility check the draft is missing for the recommended path. Whether the lighter path makes the date depends on (a) the testing window the auditor actually wants, (b) starting before January, and (c) the size of the billing access-path inventory.
evidence.limitations: The date arithmetic and capacity figures are the researcher's (11 Nov 2026 to 31 Jan 2027) and should be recomputed downstream. The 3-month window is an assumption from E17/E19, not a stated requirement of AF-2026-09. No effort estimate exists for any component.

evidence.claim: The supplied materials do not state: the audit framework behind AF-2026-09 (SOX/ICFR, SOC 2, internal audit or other); whether an operating-effectiveness period is required and how long; the database engine and version; whether the Rails monolith uses one database credential (and whether that credential is superuser or table owner); or the Rails version. None of these could be found externally.
evidence.applicability: D1 and D4. These facts decide whether the restricted-role approach works directly (PostgreSQL GRANT and pgAudit) and what go-live date the lighter path has to hit.
evidence.limitations: Internal or auditor-held information.

evidence.claim: The static analysis of billing coupling (partial, 2026-10) found 214 files referencing the Billing:: namespace. Shared DB tables between billing and other domains are 'not yet analysed'. Background jobs touching invoices number 'at least 17 (scan incomplete)'.
evidence.applicability: G2, G3 and C4. The main scope drivers are unquantified, so an exact estimate cannot be justified.
evidence.limitations: The analysis is partial. Shared tables and write paths outside billing are unknown, and the job count is a lower bound. A file reference count does not measure coupling depth.

evidence.claim: Practitioner guidance on strangler-fig extractions says application-level dual writes risk data discrepancies, and that outbox or change-data-capture patterns are safer. Shared-database sync bridges should be time-boxed or they tend to become permanent. Migrating data ownership is called the most dangerous step and is best done last.
evidence.applicability: G2 and C2/C4. Phases 2 (dual-write ledger) and 3 (invoice cutover) carry the most risk. Their effort depends on the unanalysed shared tables (E4). The source does not say anything about whether these phases can be compressed or about headcount; any 'hard to compress' claim is planner inference, not from this source.
evidence.limitations: Practitioner blogs, opinion rather than standards. Search snippets only, not fetched. There is no quantitative effort data and nothing on schedule compressibility.

evidence.claim: For SOC 2 Type II, several sources state that the AICPA sets no explicit minimum observation period. In practice 3 months is described as the industry-standard minimum accepted by most auditors (Bastion), often used for a first report. About 6 months is commonly recommended for a first Type II, and shorter periods get more scrutiny from buyers.
evidence.applicability: D4, G1 and C6. If AF-2026-09's auditor expects Type II-style operating evidence, controls have to run for a period before the deadline, and 3 months is the shortest commonly accepted window. Counting back 3 months from 30 April 2027 would put go-live at about 31 January 2027. A 6-month window would have needed go-live by about 31 October 2026, which is already past on 11 Nov 2026. This date arithmetic is the researcher's and should be rechecked downstream.
evidence.limitations: Vendor and consultancy blogs, not the AICPA itself; snippets only (the bastion.tech fetch failed: host not allowed). AF-2026-09 does not say whether the audit is SOC 2, SOX/ICFR, internal audit or something else, and it names no testing period (E1). The window is set by agreement with the auditor.

evidence.claim: For SOX/ICFR remediation, sources say a remediated or newly designed control must operate for a 'sufficient period of time' before management or auditors can conclude it is effective, and a newly designed control that has not operated long enough cannot support a conclusion that a weakness is remediated. The length is a judgement call. Practitioner blogs say that in practice most auditors expect at least one full quarter of operation, or 'typically a minimum of 3 months'. Sources also note that late go-lives leave no operating period for testing before year end.
evidence.applicability: D4. This supports a go-live target of roughly end of January 2027 for the lighter controls (one quarter before 30 April 2027) if the auditor wants operating evidence. Earlier is better if quarterly controls such as access reviews have to show more than one occurrence.
evidence.limitations: Search snippets from practitioner and consultancy sources. The SEC 2007 interpretive guidance and PCAOB AS 2201 were not inspected. The search summary did not reliably say which source gave the 'one quarter' versus the '3 months' figure, so I kept this at INFERRED even though several domains appear. It applies only if the audit is ICFR-type.
